name: DSIP
summary: A nine-amino-acid peptide, also called emideltide, first found in rabbit brain blood and taken in hopes of better sleep; evidence that it works is weak.
what_it_is: DSIP (delta sleep-inducing peptide), or emideltide, is a chain of nine amino acids first found in blood draining from rabbits' brains and later made in the lab. FDA found it is not a registered medicine in any country it searched, and it is not FDA-approved. It can cross from the blood into the brain, but enzymes in blood and tissue break it down within minutes.

evidence.why: Small studies from the 1980s and 1990s, most with under 20 people; two small placebo-controlled trials found little or no sleep benefit, and FDA identified no data supporting effectiveness.

status_us.label: Not FDA-approved; advisers voted against compounding
status_us.note: FDA dropped emideltide from its Category 2 safety-risk list in April 2026 after the nomination was withdrawn, which did not make it legal to compound. In July 2026 FDA's advisers voted 6-7 against adding it to the 503A compounding list, in line with FDA staff advice, and no peptide had been added to that list as of mid-October 2026.

benefits.claim: Better sleep continuity reported in small early studies of adults with chronic insomnia, mostly from one research group
Fewer withdrawal signs reported in an uncontrolled study of inpatients withdrawing from alcohol or opioids
Fewer sleep attacks reported in a single case of narcolepsy

risks.risk: Drop in blood pressure at the first injection, seen in 2 of 107 people in a 1984 withdrawal study
Minor effects such as sweating, headache, nausea and dizziness, in 9 of 107 people in the same study
Anxiety and marked insomnia returning after stopping, reported in withdrawal studies
Possible immune reactions to peptide clumps or impurities, which FDA says injection under the skin may increase
No toxicity or addiction-potential studies, and no safety data for injection under the skin

avoid_if: Low blood pressure, or taking medicines that lower blood pressure
Going through opioid or alcohol withdrawal (proven, supervised treatments exist)
Insomnia or narcolepsy that a clinician has not yet evaluated (approved treatments exist)

before: General health check, including blood pressure
labs.why: No evidence-based monitoring exists for DSIP; low blood pressure was reported in one older study.

studies.title: FDA Evaluation of Emideltide – Related Bulk Drug Substances
studies.people: Published studies in adults with insomnia (6 to 18 people each), one narcolepsy case and two opioid-withdrawal studies
studies.finding: FDA found the studies small and poorly controlled, with two small placebo-controlled insomnia trials showing little benefit, and identified no data supporting effectiveness for insomnia, narcolepsy or opioid withdrawal.

studies.title: Emideltide-related Bulk Drug Substances: Emideltide (Free Base) and Emideltide Acetate
studies.people: 107 people in a 1984 withdrawal study, plus FDA adverse event database search
studies.finding: FDA judged human safety insufficiently characterized: a few people had low blood pressure or minor effects, the FDA database held no reports, and no toxicity studies exist.

ask_your_clinician: What might be causing my sleep problem, and should I be checked for conditions like sleep apnea?
Would an approved sleep treatment or therapy for insomnia suit me better?
Is my blood pressure low enough that a further drop could be a problem?

notes_for_editor: The original 1980s and 1990s papers were not opened directly (PubMed was unreachable); study details come from FDA's 2026 briefing document and meeting slides, which reviewed them. The advisory vote was 6 yes to 7 no with 1 abstention, and FDA staff also recommended against. Status key is not_approved: emideltide is on no FDA compounding list and FDA found no country where it is registered. A pending HHS/FDA interim access policy for 'certain peptides' (under White House review since October 14, 2026) has not named the peptides it covers. The seed's 'stress-hormone modulation' claim and its 1983 'Effects of DSIP in man' citation were not verified and were dropped.
